# Adverse Outcomes Associated With Short‐Acting Beta‐Agonist Overuse in Asthma: A Systematic Review and Meta‐Analysis

**Authors:** Chia‐Ling Tsao; Shu‐Yen Chan; Meng‐Hsun Lee; Tina Yi Jin Hsieh; Wanda Phipatanakul; Hana B. Ruran; Kevin Sheng‐Kai Ma

**Affiliations:** 1 Center for Global Health, Perelman School of Medicine University of Pennsylvania Philadelphia Pennsylvania USA | 2 School of Medicine Chung Shan Medical University Taichung Taiwan | 3 Department of Internal Medicine Weiss Memorial Hospital Chicago Illinois USA | 4 Department of Internal Medicine Maimonides Medical Center Brooklyn New York USA | 5 Department of Biomedical Informatics Harvard Medical School Boston Massachusetts USA | 6 Division of Immunology Boston Children's Hospital, Harvard Medical School Boston Massachusetts USA | 7 Case Western Reserve University School of Medicine Cleveland Ohio USA

## Abstract

The 2019 Global Initiative for Asthma (GINA) report no longer recommended short‐acting beta‐agonists (SABA) monotherapy due to associated complications and a lack of anti‐inflammatory properties. This systematic review and meta‐analysis aimed to evaluate adverse outcomes associated with SABA overuse in patients with asthma.

PubMed, Cochrane Library, EMBASE, and Web of Science databases were searched for studies on SABA overuse (≥ 3 SABA canisters/year) in patients with asthma, from 1981 to November 2023. Randomized controlled trials (RCTs), cohort studies, and cross‐sectional studies were included. Pooled risk ratios (RRs) were calculated for dichotomous measures of all‐cause mortality and acute exacerbations using random‐effects models and Mantel‐Haenszel weighting. Subgroup analyses were conducted based on study design.

Out of 626 records, 27 studies (2 RCTs, 1 prospective cohort study, 12 retrospective cohort studies, and 12 cross‐sectional studies) were included. SABA overuse (≥ 3 SABA canisters/year) was associated with significantly higher mortality (2743 of 130,629 in the overuse group versus 3534 of 300,451 in controls; RR = 2.04, 95% confidence interval, CI = 1.37–3.04; p < 0.001) and a significantly higher rate of acute exacerbations (60,320 of 165,271 in the overuse group versus 84,439 of 376,845 in controls; RR = 1.93, 95% CI = 1.24–3.03; p < 0.001). An increased risk of acute exacerbations was observed in retrospective cohort studies (RR = 1.88, 95% CI = 1.43–2.47; p < 0.001) and cross‐sectional studies (RR = 2.23, 95% CI = 1.04–4.77; p < 0.001).

SABA overuse was associated with increased rates of mortality and acute exacerbations in patients with asthma, supporting guidelines that advise against SABA monotherapy in asthma management.

## Introduction

Asthma is a common airway disease that affects approximately 262 million individuals worldwide and contributes to more than 1000 deaths per day [1]. The prevalence of asthma symptoms varies between different age groups and countries and is reported to be higher in children and adolescents and in countries with higher household incomes [2]. Asthma is a heterogeneous disease characterized by bronchial hyperresponsiveness and chronic airway inflammation and primarily affects the lower respiratory tract, causing symptoms such as cough, wheezing, dyspnea, and chest tightness [3, 4]. These symptoms can be triggered and exacerbated by respiratory tract infections, allergens, exercise, or pollutant exposure [5]. Besides causing respiratory symptoms, asthma has been reported to be associated with multiple comorbidities. Atopic diseases, gastroesophageal reflux disease (GERD), obstructive sleep apnea (OSA), obesity, and psychiatric disorders are among the most common [6]. According to the World Health Organization (WHO), asthma accounts for 21.6 million disability‐adjusted life years (DALYs), ranking 34th among the leading causes of burden of disease and is responsible for a fifth of total DALYs from chronic respiratory diseases [4, 7, 8]. Due to its prevalence, asthma and its comorbidities impose a significant burden not only on patients' quality of life and financial situation but also on the entire healthcare system.

Asthma management aims to control clinical symptoms, reduce future exacerbations, and prevent fixed airway obstruction. Decreasing comorbidities and minimizing adverse effects from medications are as well important in the treatment course [3]. Short‐acting beta‐agonists (SABA) have a rapid‐onset bronchodilatory effect and have been used to treat acute asthma symptoms for the past 30 years [3]. In 2019, the Global Initiative for Asthma (GINA) introduced a novel treatment strategy. SABA monotherapy was no longer recommended for mild asthma. Instead, a combination of inhaled corticosteroids (ICS) and formoterol inhalers was recommended for all patients with asthma, to relieve acute symptoms and reduce chronic airway inflammation concomitantly [9]. Meanwhile, ICS‐formoterol has been shown to significantly reduce the risk of exacerbations compared to SABA monotherapy [10]. Likewise, ICS‐albuterol has been considered a choice of asthma rescue therapy after the approval of the US Food and Drug Administration [11]. In the MANDALA trial, as‐needed albuterol‐budesonide 180/160 mg pressurized metered‐dose inhalers significantly reduced the risk of severe exacerbations by 27% compared with as‐needed albuterol alone [12]. Despite updated GINA recommendations, SABA overuse (≥ 3 canisters annually) remains prevalent [13]. The global study by the SABA use IN Asthma program (SABINA) has demonstrated the disease burden associated with SABA overuse among patients with asthma across multiple countries [14, 15, 16, 17]. Studies indicate that SABA overuse is often linked to ICS underuse and inadequate control of underlying airway inflammation. In addition, growing evidence reveals that overuse of SABA is associated with an increased risk of acute exacerbations and mortality [13, 14, 15, 16, 17, 18].

While numerous observational studies highlight the association between SABA overuse and increased asthma complications, high‐quality evidence remains limited. The aim of this systematic review and meta‐analysis was to substantiate the association between SABA overuse and increased rates of mortality and acute exacerbations among the asthma population. We hope that the synthesis of current evidence from this study can serve as a catalyst for improving prescribing patterns among clinicians, influencing guidelines and policy formulations, and ultimately reducing the global burden of asthma.

## Materials and Methods

### Search Strategy and Eligibility Criteria

A comprehensive literature search was conducted to include peer‐reviewed original articles published from 1981 to November 2023 that provided primary data comparing outcomes among patients with asthma who excessively used or were prescribed SABA (≥ 3 SABA canisters/year) with those who did not (< 3 SABA canisters/year) as the control group. The literature we searched for primarily focused on single‐use SABA inhalers, such as albuterol or levalbuterol, and excluded combination inhalers or nebulized formulations of ICS, such as budesonide. Primary outcomes were acute exacerbations and all‐cause mortality. This search was performed across multiple databases, including PubMed, Embase, Web of Science, and Cochrane Database of Systematic Reviews. The search strategy used the following keywords and Boolean logic: (“SABA” OR “Short‐acting β2‐agonists” OR “Short‐acting β2‐agonist”) AND “overuse”. A review of the reference lists was also conducted in relevant reviews to identify any potentially eligible articles that may have been missed during the initial search. Inclusion criteria were original randomized controlled trials (RCTs), prospective or retrospective cohort studies, and cross‐sectional studies published in English.

### Data Extraction and Screening Process

Two independent authors (C.T. and T.H.) conducted the initial screening by assessing the titles and abstracts of the identified articles. Following this, another pair of independent authors (S.C. and M.L.) thoroughly reviewed the full texts of articles identified as potentially eligible based on predetermined criteria. Conflicts or disagreements during the screening process were resolved through discussion and consensus with a third reviewer (K.S.M.). The data extraction included characteristics of the study populations such as demographics, study designs, baseline severity of asthma, reasons for SABA prescription, dosage and frequency of SABA treatment, prior or concomitant treatments, including ICS and long‐acting beta‐agonists (LABA), and outcomes such as all‐cause mortality, incident cases of acute exacerbations, sepsis or septic shock, and healthcare utilization, including emergency department (ED) visits or hospitalizations.

### Statistical Analysis

To evaluate the effects of SABA overuse on acute exacerbations and all‐cause mortality, meta‐analyses were performed employing the Dersimonian and Laird method. Pooled risk ratios (RRs) were calculated using random‐effects models with Mantel‐Haenszel weighting and a zero‐cell correction of 0.5 for dichotomous outcomes. A subgroup analysis was performed to evaluate the effect size across studies with different study designs (retrospective cohort studies versus cross‐sectional studies) as a potential source of heterogeneity. The I 2 statistic was used to assess the heterogeneity between studies included in the meta‐analysis. Funnel plots and Egger's test were used to estimate publication bias. Statistical analyses were performed using Stata, version 16.1. Statistical significance was defined as two‐tailed p ≤ 0.05.

### Quality Assessment of Included Studies

Two independent reviewers (C.T. and S.C.) assessed study quality using assessment tools tailored to each study design, including the Risk of Bias 2 (ROB 2) tool for RCTs and the Newcastle‐Ottawa Scale (NOS) for observational studies. Disagreements were resolved through discussion with the third author. Specifically, with the ROB 2 tool, five domains were evaluated: the randomization process, deviations from intended interventions, missing outcome data, measurement of the outcome, and selection of the reported result [19]. If two or more of these domains were rated as having a high risk of bias during the assessment, the overall risk‐of‐bias judgment for the study was considered high. Observational studies were assessed using NOS, which employs a “star system” to rate each domain for risk of bias (low, moderate, high, or unclear): the selection of study groups, the comparability of groups, and the ascertainment of either the exposure or the outcome of interest [20]. A higher score reflected higher study quality.

## Results

### Characteristics and Summary of the Included Studies

The initial search yielded 626 citations, and after removing duplicates, 470 articles were selected for comprehensive full‐text review. Out of these, 443 articles were excluded for various reasons: 277 were not relevant to SABA overuse in terms of study contents or outcomes, 42 were not clinical trials, cohort studies, or cross‐sectional studies, 18 lacked full‐text availability, 9 did not focus on patients with asthma, 75 either did not involve SABA overuse as an exposure or did not report the dosage or frequency of SABA, and 22 were excluded for other reasons, including being published in languages other than English. Consequently, 27 studies met the eligibility criteria for inclusion in this systematic review (Figure 1).

*FIGURE 1: Flow diagram of the study selection process following the Preferred Reporting Items for Systematic Reviews and Meta‐analyses (PRISMA) guidelines.*

Among the 27 eligible studies, there were 2 RCTs, 1 prospective cohort study, 12 retrospective cohort studies, and 12 cross‐sectional studies. Definitions of cases of SABA overuse and controls in each study and adverse outcomes associated with SABA overuse were summarized (Table 1). The pooled sample size comprised patients with asthma, ranging in age from 3 to 99, with reported information for individuals characterized by SABA overuse. Sample sizes of each study varied from 100 [24] to 1,033,564 [35]. Several extensive, multi‐center, multi‐country studies were part of this review, with 27 studies originating from countries across six continents: Europe (n = 10), North America (n = 5), Asia (n = 7), Oceania (n = 2), and three studies spanning multiple continents (n = 3). Adverse outcomes associated with SABA overuse included acute exacerbations, all‐cause mortality, healthcare utilization, including emergency visits and hospitalizations, sepsis, and septic shock (Table 1).

### Acute Exacerbations Associated with SABA Overuse in Patients with Asthma

Nine studies, including four retrospective cohort studies [13, 17, 30, 36], one RCT [24], and four cross‐sectional studies [15, 27, 31, 37, 43], were pooled to assess the association between SABA overuse and acute exacerbations (Table 2). The data from Bateman et al. [15] overlapped with other studies, including those by Montero‐Arias et al. [42], Avddev et al. [37], and Alzaabi et al. [38], as shown in Table 1. To avoid introducing duplicate records, we included only the data from Bateman et al. in our meta‐analysis. The cumulative participant counts totaled 165,271 in the SABA overuse group and 376,845 in the control group. Within these cohorts, 60,320 (36.50%) patients in the SABA overuse group experienced acute exacerbations, whereas only 84,439 (22.41%) of patients in the control group developed acute exacerbations. Random‐effects meta‐analysis revealed a statistically significant increase in the risk of acute exacerbations among patients in the SABA overuse group compared to the control group (RR: 1.93, 95% CI: 1.24–3.03, I 2 = 99.9%) (Figure 2A). Stratified by study designs, it was demonstrated that SABA overuse was associated with a significantly increased risk of acute exacerbations compared to controls within retrospective cohort studies (RR: 1.88, 95% CI: 1.43–2.47, I 2 = 99.2%) (Figure 2B) and cross‐sectional studies (RR: 2.23, 95% CI: 1.04–4.77, I 2 = 99.7%). No statistically significant associations were observed in the included RCT (RR: 1.14, 95% CI: 0.95–1.36).

### All‐Cause Mortality Associated with SABA Overuse in Patients with Asthma

Pooled data from two retrospective cohort studies and one cross‐sectional study were retrieved to evaluate the effect of SABA overuse on all‐cause mortality (Table 2). One cohort study found that 30% of the 365,324 included patients with asthma overused SABA (≥ 3 canisters annually). A total of 1365 (0.54%) patients in the control group died, whereas the SABA overuse group had 1199 (1.07%) deaths [13]. Another cohort study involving 59,533 patients with asthma found that 1255 out of 8465 (14.83%) patients who overused SABA died, compared to 1942 out of 17,736 (10.95%) deaths among those who used 1–2 canisters [36]. A cross‐sectional study found that 289 out of 11,340 (2.55%) patients who were exposed to SABA overuse died, compared to 227 out of 28,215 (0.8%) deaths among those who used 0‐2 canisters [43]. The random‐effects model meta‐analysis comprising 130,629 participants in the SABA overuse group and 300,451 in the control group suggested that SABA overuse was associated with a significantly increased all‐cause mortality rate (RR: 2.04, 95% CI: 1.37–3.04, I 2 = 98.3%) (Figure 2C).

### Assessment of Risk of Bias and Publication Bias

## Discussion

Large‐scale studies have shown that the overuse of SABA in asthma may increase the risks of disease exacerbations, asthma‐related hospitalizations, and mortality [13, 14, 15, 16, 17, 35, 42]. The present study is the first systematic review and meta‐analysis to investigate the association between SABA overuse and adverse outcomes. The risks of all‐cause mortality and acute exacerbations were significantly increased in the SABA overuse group. These results provide high‐level evidence supporting current asthma treatment guidelines.

The 2019 GINA recommendation states that patients receiving three or more SABA canisters per year are at an increased risk of ED visits. Following the updated GINA recommendation, most studies define SABA overuse as more than three prescribed inhalers per year, which approximates 600 puffs per year or an average of ≥ 1.5 puffs a day [9, 45, 46]. Despite this, there is no consensus on the definition of SABA overuse, and different professional societies apply varying cut‐off points. For example, in 2021 the Canadian Thoracic Society (CTS) defined SABA overuse as using more than two inhalers of SABA in one year [47]. It is important to clarify the threshold of SABA use that significantly increases mortality rates and the risk of acute exacerbations. However, original data on SABA dosing are necessary to enable subgroup analysis, yet most of the studies included in this systematic review and meta‐analysis do not provide such information. To improve the safety of asthma care and prevent complications, additional research should aim to establish a specific cutoff point for SABA overuse.

The SABINA program comprised four major studies, including SABINA I, SABINA II, SABINA III, and SABINA +, which enrolled more than one million patients with asthma across multiple continents. While some nuances existed across these studies, they shared common study design principles and objectives, ensuring cohesive findings [35]. The overarching goal of this program was to examine the real‐world use of SABA treatments in patients with asthma and the associated outcomes. The collective body of research underscored the persistent global issue of SABA overuse and overprescription, which imposes a significant burden on global healthcare. Among the 1,033,564 patients with asthma in Europe and North America, a notable 40.2% were found to use or be prescribed three or more SABA canisters annually, with prevalence ranging from 26.0% in the Netherlands to 63.2% in Canada. In another pillar of the study involving 8351 patients recruited from 24 countries, 38% of patients were found to overuse SABA inhalers. Similarly, the prevalence varied widely across countries, ranging from 7.6% in South Korea to 74.9% in South Africa [13, 14, 15, 16, 17, 35, 42, 48]. The variation could be due to different practice types, insurance policies, sociodemographic parameters, and access to healthcare in different countries [49].

SABA have been a mainstay in asthma treatment since their introduction in the 1950s [50]. The adverse effects of SABA treatment in patients with asthma have long been reported and are under extensive investigation. A cohort analysis published in 1994 revealed an association between beta‐agonist use and excess mortality [51]. Another early report noted a significant association between asthma‐related ED visits or hospital admissions and SABA prescriptions, which helped usher in the concept that SABA prescription fills can be used as a marker of asthma morbidity [52]. It was discovered that the use of SABA nebulizers was associated with poor asthma control or acute exacerbations, which presented as asthma‐related ED visits and hospitalizations [53]. As more studies have been done to explore the association, there is growing evidence showing the risk of overreliance on SABA. In 2019, a fundamental change was introduced in GINA reports. Since then, SABA monotherapy has no longer been recommended for mild asthma for associated complications. Instead, anti‐inflammatory reliever (AIR) therapy containing ICS‐formoterol is preferred and recommended in step 1–2 asthma treatment. Moreover, ICS‐formoterol has been recommended as maintenance and reliever therapy (MART) for step 3–5 asthma management after studies showed ICS‐formoterol significantly reduced severe exacerbations and hospital admissions compared to SABA alone [9, 10, 54, 55].

Treatment with SABA remains safe when used in limited amounts or prescribed alongside ICS. The adverse effects of SABA use primarily result from excessive dosage. In the SABINA program, the positive association between SABA overuse and severe exacerbations or deaths has been reported [13, 14, 15, 16, 17, 35, 42, 46, 48]. The study conducted in Sweden divided the patients into four different groups based on the number of canisters used per year (≤ 2; 3–5; 6–10; and ≥ 11 canisters/year) and analyzed the outcomes after adjusting for confounding factors. Importantly, both the risk of exacerbations and mortality risk increased with an increasing number of SABA canisters used in a dose‐dependent manner [14]. The analysis of patients from Spain revealed a significant dose‐dependent pattern between the number of SABA canisters collected and asthma exacerbation risk [43]. Another meta‐analysis including 24 RCTs investigated the safety of SABA relievers regardless of whether SABA were overused and showed that appropriate use of SABA monotherapy within the prescribed limit may not contribute to increased mortality or acute exacerbations [56]. Hence, the complications caused by SABA appear to be dose‐dependent and are seen more often in those who overuse SABA.

SABA overuse may also be linked to insufficient use of concomitant ICS. Long‐term adherence to ICS is reported to be poor in 76% of uncontrolled asthmatics [57]. Evidence suggests that poor control of asthma, characterized by high SABA usage, results from patients' lack of adherence to ICS [58]. According to a meta‐analysis of 19 studies, 24% of exacerbations and 60% of asthma‐related hospitalizations can be attributed to poor adherence to ICS [59]. Therefore, SABA overuse may reflect inadequate disease control due to insufficient ICS use, rather than directly causing exacerbations.

The mechanism of SABA overuse‐related exacerbations or mortality is still poorly understood. Possible explanations include uncontrolled underlying disease, SABA‐masked disease severity, and delayed medical attention. Furthermore, airway inflammation and bronchial hyperresponsiveness due to the overprescription of SABA may lead to a higher exacerbation risk and mortality [60]. Beta‐agonist‐induced tachycardia and hypokalemia can play important roles as well [61]. In addition to SABA, LABA have raised similar concerns for increasing asthma mortality. The Salmeterol Multicenter Asthma Research Trial, a randomized, double‐blind, placebo‐controlled study that evaluated the safety of LABA, showed a 4‐fold increase in asthma‐related deaths with salmeterol in patients with unstable asthma [62]. By contrast, the addition of salmeterol to fluticasone propionate in a combination inhaler has been shown to significantly reduce the risk for severe asthma exacerbations by 21% [63]. LABA with ICS is considered a safe choice for mild asthma treatment. Further investigations are needed to explore the underlying mechanisms connecting beta‐agonists with increased morbidity and mortality in patients with asthma.

### Study Strengths and Limitations

This systematic review and meta‐analysis, comprising 27 studies from multiple countries, represents a comprehensive assessment of the relationship between SABA overuse and adverse outcomes. One of its strengths is the inclusion of both RCTs and real‐world evidence from global populations, which provided compelling level 1 evidence that underscored the adverse outcomes associated with SABA overuse, thereby reinforcing current clinical guidelines.

Limitations of this study include the lack of RCTs, which are impractical in the context of SABA overuse, and potential biases in observational studies. For instance, residual and unmeasured confounders such as lack of control of disease, environmental factors, and medication adherence may be present in those studies, despite efforts of adjustments for available variables, including baseline severity of asthma. Beyond acute exacerbations and mortality, immediate adverse effects such as tachycardia and hypokalemia after SABA overuse may warrant further investigation.

SABA can be administered through various routes, including metered‐dose inhalers (MDIs) and nebulized solutions [64]. A randomized controlled trial in the US found that the strongest association with poor asthma outcomes was linked to the use of nebulized SABA, suggesting that the route of administration may have prognostic significance [53]. This suggests that the route of administration may be an important factor that requires investigation. Another influencing factor is the type of ICS used, which may impact outcomes associated with SABA [65]. A retrospective cohort study demonstrated that differences between specific ICS molecules, such as mometasone furoate and fluticasone propionate, could affect adherence and subsequent SABA use [66]. Therefore, specific molecules should be evaluated individually rather than grouped collectively. Nevertheless, the studies included in our analysis did not provide sufficient stratified outcome data, making it challenging to conduct subgroup analyses based on specific molecules. Future research should clarify whether different molecules exhibit distinct safety profiles.

Another limitation involves variations in inclusion criteria and differences in adherence to asthma treatment guidelines across the included studies. Differences in healthcare practices, including prescribing patterns for SABA, may have influenced the reported outcomes. Moreover, evolving guidelines over time have led to studies conducted in different eras following distinct protocols. These discrepancies, including variations in the definitions of overuse or overprescription and differences in the reference groups used for comparison, likely contributed to the heterogeneity observed in the current meta‐analysis. Furthermore, most studies included in this meta‐analysis either followed the British Thoracic Society (BTS) 2016 asthma guideline or the 2018 GINA recommendation, both of which do not advise against SABA monotherapy. While this may not alter the association between SABA overuse and adverse outcomes, it highlights a historical context of greater SABA overprescription and overreliance.

## Conclusion

This systematic review and meta‐analysis demonstrates a significant association between SABA overuse and heightened risks of acute exacerbations and mortality. These findings align with previous literature and offer stronger evidence supporting current asthma treatment guidelines, which recommend SABA in combination with ICS or as needed in select populations. Importantly, the confounding factor of low concomitant ICS use may lead to adverse effects of SABA overuse. Research is needed to elucidate the mechanisms underlying SABA overuse‐related adverse effects, and to support healthcare providers and policymakers in implementing regulations to reduce the asthma‐related disease burden associated with SABA overuse.
